title: The Word is the Guru
hookLine: the yogis ask who Nanak's guru is, and he answers: the Word is the Guru, attention is the disciple

cards: Who did you study with? Ask a classical musician and you'll often hear a name, and behind that name another, a line of teachers going back through the years. In that world, your teacher is part of who you are.
The yogis Nanak met also spoke of teachers and their disciples. So, in the Sidh Gosht, they ask the obvious question. What is the root of all this?
Who is your guru? Whose disciple are you?

teach.b: Here a few of the original words are worth hearing: sabad guroo, surat dhun chelaa. Sabad is the Word, the shabad. Guroo, the Guru.
Surat is attention, awareness. Dhun is the tune, the strain of the music. Chelaa is the disciple.

So, in paraphrase: the Word is the Guru, and attention tuned to it is the disciple. He goes on: speaking the unspoken, he stays unattached, and through all the ages, the Lord of the world is his Guru.
Look at what he doesn't say.
He gives no human name, no line of teachers to check. The yogis asked for a person, and he gives them a relationship. On one side, the Word.
On the other, your own attention, tuned to it, the way a string is tuned to a note. A guru, in this answer, isn't someone you trace back. It's something you listen to now.

And the disciple isn't a body sitting at someone's feet; it's the part of you that pays attention. So anyone who listens can be a disciple, today, wherever they are. The teaching reaches whoever tunes in.
It also explains something about Sikh life.
Sikhs today bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, a book of hymns, as the Guru. A visitor seeing that for the first time may be surprised.
In this stanza, Guru Nanak had already answered the yogis that way: the Word is the Guru.

how: Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru, bowing before it in the gurdwara, and often cite 'sabad guroo surat dhun chelaa' when explaining why the Word, not a human lineage, is the Guru.

games.q: what does “the word is the guru” mean?
o: Nanak naming the yogi teacher who first trained him as a boy
Nanak's answer: the Word is Guru, and tuned attention the disciple
a rule that every Sikh must choose a living human teacher

games.q: what's inside the line — tap the pairs.
p: the tune, the strain of music

s: Nanak answers the yogis with the name of his human teacher
he names no person: the Word is the Guru, attention is the disciple.
in the stanza, the disciple is attention tuned to the Word
surat dhun chelaa: attention, tuned, is the disciple.
Sikhs today bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru
the book of hymns is honored as the Guru, as this answer already pointed toward.

games.q: you're a yogi, and your own teacher has a name and a lineage. you ask Nanak: who is your guru, whose disciple are you? what does he say?
o: he names his teacher and his teacher's teacher.
the Word is the Guru, and tuned attention is the disciple.
he has no need of any guru.
games.why: sabad guroo, surat dhun chelaa: no human name, but a Guru all the same, and a disciple anyone can be.

practice: If you can, play a shabad you love, quietly, or let one line of Gurbani you know sit in the silence, or simply Waheguru, and be the disciple in the stanza: not a body at someone's feet, just attention resting on the sound the way a string settles on a note.
When it drifts, that's the string going slack; bring it gently back into tune, without trying to understand every word. If you pray, the listening itself can be the prayer.

wordCard.voice: The Word is the Guru. Sabad guroo, surat dhun chelaa: Nanak's answer to the yogis, the Word as Guru and tuned attention as the disciple. Today's word.

orig.note: the Word is the Guru; attention tuned to it is the disciple.

carryVoice: Your line: the word is guru. Anyone who listens can be a disciple. Go gently.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ramkali, Mahala 1, Sidh Gosht, pauris 43–44, Ang 942–943 (who is your guru; sabad guroo surat dhun chelaa)
